# Abstract

Secure land tenure is widely assumed to raise agricultural productivity by strengthening investment incentives and easing access to credit, and land titling has become a common instrument of agricultural policy across sub-Saharan Africa. Whether ownership itself improves farm performance remains unsettled, in part because aggregate productivity comparisons cannot separate the technology a farmer is able to reach from the efficiency with which that technology is used. Here we analyse `r fmt_num(N_ALL, 0)` farm households observed across five rounds of the Ghana Living Standards Survey, combining statistical matching with a meta-stochastic frontier that recovers these two components separately. Landowners and matched non-owners differ by less than one percentage point in overall efficiency, a difference that is statistically significant but economically small. Disaggregating by tenure form reverses the expected pattern: documented owners and holders of transferable rights fall below comparable non-owners in meta-frontier efficiency, and owners lead only within particular routes of land access. The direction of the ownership gap thus depends on which dimension of tenure is measured. Formal ownership appears neither necessary nor sufficient for superior farm performance, suggesting that titling alone is unlikely to raise productivity without complementary input, credit, and market reforms.
